problem: Embodied Question Answering in House3D requires hundreds of primitive actions, partial observability, and a sparse answer-based reward. Flat or weakly hierarchical navigators such as PACMAN from Das et al. find this hard to learn with RL, and their decisions are not interpretable.
motivation: Humans break long tasks into semantic subgoals (exit bedroom, go to kitchen, find object). A hierarchy of this kind shortens the horizon over which the final answer reward must propagate. It also allows modular pretraining from expert demonstrations and exposes interpretable intermediate goals. EQA questions have an explicit target object, and House3D provides room and object annotations, so expert shortest paths can be automatically 'lifted' into subgoal sequences for supervision.
key_idea: A two-level Neural Modular Controller: a GRU master policy emits semantic subgoals ⟨task, argument⟩ (exit-room, find-room[X], find-object[Y], answer), and argument-conditioned GRU sub-policies execute each one as primitive actions. Both levels are trained by hierarchical behavior cloning on automatically segmented shortest-path trajectories, then fine-tuned with A3C.
insight: The hierarchy alone does not help: NMC (BC) performs about the same as PACMAN (BC), with no consistent winner across spawn distances. The gains appear only after A3C fine-tuning, where the master explores in subgoal space over compressed horizons and sub-policies learn to recover from their own errors. For every sub-policy task, the sub-policy training curves (Fig. 3) show BC is more sample-efficient than A3C from scratch, and BC+A3C clearly beats both, nearly doubling BC success on some tasks. The BC advantage is larger for harder tasks, where a random policy does worse. In the full table, at T-50 NMC (BC+A3C) enters the target room less often than PACMAN (%r_↲ 10.40 vs 18.83) and has larger d_min (6.95 vs 6.38), yet it has lower d_T and higher accuracy. So the gains are partly due to always stopping (%stop 100%) closer to the target, not only to reaching the target room more often.
method: Subgoal space: 4 tasks (exit-room, find-room, find-object, answer); find-room takes one of 12 room types and find-object one of 50 object types, giving 64 subgoals; each subgoal has a success criterion (e.g. find-object = stop within 0.75 m of the target).

Master policy: single-layer GRU (hidden 1048) taking question encoding (128-d), current frame CNN feature (128-d) and an embedding of the previous subgoal (32-d); outputs a distribution over the 64 subgoals plus a value estimate; called again each time a sub-policy stops or hits its step limit.

Sub-policies: single-layer GRUs whose parameters are shared per task, conditioned on a learned argument embedding (room or object); inputs are frame feature (128-d), previous action embedding (32-d) and argument embedding; outputs forward / turn-left / turn-right / stop plus a value estimate.

Automatic subgoal extraction: shortest-path expert trajectories are segmented at room transitions using House3D room/object bounding boxes (floor plan viewed as a room–doorway graph). find-object is tagged only once inside the target room; exit-room is tagged only when the current room has out-degree 1, otherwise find-room is used.

Hierarchical behavior cloning: cross-entropy losses decompose into independent problems; the master is trained on expert subgoal sequences (assuming perfect sub-policies) and each sub-policy on its segmented action trajectories.

A3C + GAE fine-tuning (8 threads, 4 GPUs): sub-policies are fine-tuned independently with a 0/1 success reward, shaped rewards from the change in navigable distance, and a -0.02 collision penalty. The master is then fine-tuned with the trained sub-policies, using the answer-correctness terminal reward plus distance shaping. A curriculum samples start states along expert trajectories and shrinks the sampling prefix α by 0.9 whenever success exceeds 40%.

Perception and QA are kept identical to PACMAN: a frozen CNN pretrained on auto-encoding, segmentation and depth provides features; the answering module (2-layer LSTM question encoder with attention over the last 5 frames) is trained on shortest-path features and frozen.

setting.backbone: GRU master policy + GRU sub-policies (trained from scratch with BC then A3C), on top of a frozen pretrained CNN encoder and frozen LSTM-attention VQA module from Das et al. (EmbodiedQA/PACMAN)
setting.training_data: EQA v1 train split (7129 questions, 648 House3D environments). Shortest-path expert trajectories are automatically segmented into subgoal sequences (N master trajectories, K>>N sub-policy trajectories) using House3D room/object bounding boxes. No extra or web data.
setting.observation: egocentric monocular RGB (first-person frames only, encoded by a frozen CNN) + question text
setting.action_space: hierarchical: master chooses among 64 semantic subgoals; sub-policies output low-level forward / turn-left / turn-right / stop
setting.privileged: none at test time (room/object annotations and shortest paths are used only for training supervision and reward shaping). Evaluation follows the EQA protocol of spawning the agent 10/30/50 primitive actions from the target along the shortest path.

numbers.backbone: GRU master + GRU sub-policies, frozen PACMAN CNN + VQA
numbers.extra: Agent spawned 10/30/50 primitive actions from target (d_0 = 1.15/4.87/9.64 m); metrics suffixed by spawn distance. Accuracy uses the frozen VQA model from Das et al.; dataset version is the updated public EQA v1 (color-label changes).

numbers.backbone: GRU master + GRU sub-policies, frozen PACMAN CNN + VQA
numbers.extra: Behavior cloning only, no A3C fine-tuning at any level. Same spawn protocol (10/30/50 actions from target).

numbers_note: EQA v1 (House3D/SUNCG) is not MP3D-EQA, so it is logged as other:EQA-v1 (House3D). %r_T = % episodes terminating in the target room; %r_enter = %r_↲, % episodes that ever entered the target room. d_Δ is defined in the text as d_T − d_0, but the printed values are positive for progress; numbers are copied as printed. Sub-policy success rates (BC vs A3C vs BC+A3C vs random, EQA v1 val) appear only as training curves in Fig. 3, with no numeric values. Master-policy BC achieves '∼48%' IoU with ground-truth subgoal sequences on val (approximate, not tabulated). PACMAN numbers were re-run by the authors on the updated dataset and differ from the original EmbodiedQA paper. ShortestPath+VQA upper bound is 56.85% accuracy.
results: On the EQA v1 test set, NMC (BC+A3C) beats the strongest baseline PACMAN (BC+REINFORCE) in answering accuracy at all spawn distances: 53.58/46.21/44.32% vs 50.21/42.26/40.76% at T-10/T-30/T-50, against a shortest-path oracle of 56.85%. It also terminates closer to the target at longer distances (d_T 3.72 vs 4.22 m at T-30, 7.94 vs 8.13 m at T-50), though PACMAN is marginally better at T-10 (1.05 vs 1.06). Without RL fine-tuning, NMC (BC) is not consistently better than PACMAN (BC), so A3C fine-tuning of the hierarchy is what drives the gain.
limitations: The subgoal vocabulary and segmentation heuristics are hand-designed and depend on House3D room/object bounding boxes and floor-plan graphs for training supervision. The approach is tied to the room/object structure of EQA questions.

Evaluation covers only House3D with agents spawned at most 50 actions (~9.6 m) from the target. At T-50, NMC reaches or ends in the target room less often than PACMAN (%r_↲ 10.40 vs 18.83; %r_T 9.28 vs 12.98) and has worse d_min, so long-range navigation remains weak.

Perception and QA modules are frozen from prior work. There are no ablations of master-policy design (e.g., argument sharing, subgoal set), and the master's subgoal prediction generalizes only moderately (~48% IoU on val).
